notes.title: What Should Change When AX Moves Across Industries?
notes.summary: What changes across industries isn't the model. It's what breaks when things fail, which rules apply, and whether the result can be undone. That's why the same summarization, search, or execution task calls for different AI permissions and verification in each industry.

notes.title: As AI writes code faster, what needs to change in software development?
notes.summary: Faster AI code generation does not speed up delivery to users when review, CI, merging, and deployment are backed up. Identify where delays occur, and track time to deployment, errors, and rework alongside code output. Drawing on company examples, this note covers development bottlenecks, responsibility for verification, and how to measure productivity.

notes.title: How can AI help clean up code?
notes.summary: A lack of recorded calls is not enough reason to delete code. Even when AI identifies cleanup candidates, their original purpose, production usage history, and dependencies on other features still need to be checked. Drawing on a Codex case study, this note covers investigating unused code, completed experiments, and slow CI jobs, making changes in small PRs, and verifying their impact.

notes.title: How should we choose a technology stack for AI search and RAG?
notes.summary: Choosing an AI search and RAG stack starts with identifying whether failures occur in candidate retrieval, ranking, or evidence lookup. This note distinguishes the roles and requirements of keyword and vector search, reranking, and SQL and graph queries, and sets out criteria for comparing accuracy and operating costs.

notes.title: As AI agents multiply, what should a company manage?
notes.summary: Creating more agents does not by itself make an AI transformation successful. Organizations need to know what each agent does, who manages it, what permissions it has, and whether it delivers results. Drawing on Gartner forecasts and examples from SKT, IBM, and Cisco, this note covers management across the agent lifecycle and criteria for keeping, improving, or retiring agents.

notes.title: How should a service behave while users wait for an AI answer?
notes.summary: The design should define whether users can do other things while waiting for an AI response and how they can check progress and results. Leaving a screen and canceling a task should be treated separately, with clear limits on what can be retried after a failure. This note covers synchronous and asynchronous processing, streaming, queues, and how response patterns and available user actions should fit the task and its state.

notes.title: Comparing IDEs — VS Code · Kiro · Cursor
notes.summary: VS Code is mix-and-match, Kiro is spec-driven, Cursor is agent-driven. A comparison of how each handles AI coding, project rules, and planning and verifying work, based on official docs.

notes.title: How autonomous should an agent be?
notes.summary: An agent's autonomy should depend on its permissions, the impact of its actions, and whether they can be reversed. Rather than requiring approval for every action, distinguish automatic execution, prior approval, and prohibited actions, and let users inspect and stop execution. This note covers placing Human-in-the-loop at points that require human judgment and intervention, and connecting those decisions to the approval experience, error recovery, and operational metrics.

notes.title: How should you design KPIs for an AI agent?
notes.summary: An agent that works accurately is not necessarily one that improves the work itself. First define the task and what counts as success, then consider review and rework time, costs, and permission compliance alongside completion rate. This note covers choosing metrics in the order of goals → success criteria → KPIs → measurement and validation → improvement.

notes.title: How can an AI agent's work continue across devices?
notes.summary: Continuing work across devices requires managing progress and the execution environment alongside conversation history. Devices should share the same task state, while defining what users can inspect and control on each device. Drawing on Copilot examples, this note covers resuming tasks, approvals and permissions, device-specific UX, and considerations when measuring usage.

notes.title: Character count couldn't evaluate a report — splitting checks between code and an LLM judge
notes.summary: Code can check formatting and required fields, but whether the content matches its evidence needs a separate evaluation. LLM Judge verdicts can vary, so automated evaluation alone cannot establish quality. This note covers the roles of code checks and LLM evaluation, when human review is needed, and what information reviewers need.

notes.title: How do you put together a tech stack for a service?
notes.summary: Choosing a tech stack means deciding on an appropriate level of complexity based on service requirements, team capabilities, and development and operating costs, rather than seeking the best technology in isolation. This note covers the requirements and constraints a PM can provide, six criteria for choosing technology, how to judge overengineering, MSA, and new tech, and ADRs for recording why you chose what you did.

notes.title: When an AI answer is wrong, how do you find where it failed?
notes.summary: Knowing that the final answer is wrong does not tell you what to fix. Step-by-step execution records (Tracing) help narrow down the cause by showing retrieval results, information passed to the model, tool calls, and final output. This note covers checking improvements and regressions against the same evaluation cases after a change, and deciding what to log.

notes.title: Why build it as an AI agent? — can you decide the next step in advance
notes.summary: Calling an LLM multiple times or using tools does not by itself mean an agent is needed. First identify whether the model needs to choose its next action based on intermediate results. If an agent is used, define what it can choose, its execution limits, and when it must stop, then compare whether it actually produces better results than a fixed workflow.

notes.title: When do you need RAG, and when does it make things worse?
notes.summary: Adding retrieval does not guarantee accurate answers. Depending on the amount and type of information needed, compare it with passing entire documents to the model or querying an API or database. When using RAG, check whether retrieval loses important conditions and whether the evidence applies to the actual question, then evaluate answer quality alongside operating costs.

notes.title: How much can we trust the patterns AI finds in data?
notes.summary: Before using a pattern found by AI to make a business decision, define what that pattern is meant to help decide. Check whether it holds under different aggregation choices, recurs in other periods, and reflects the phenomenon the data is supposed to measure. Using a customer-support example, this note distinguishes the evidence needed for observations, predictions, and staffing decisions.

notes.title: No evidence, no answer — citation checks for RAG
notes.summary: When retrieval finds no supporting evidence, answer generation can be stopped, and code can filter out citations that are not on the allowed list. But a citation existing is different from its source supporting the claim. This note covers responses when evidence is missing, citation validation rules, and what code can and cannot verify.

notes.title: Can you stop prompt injection just by fixing the prompt?
notes.summary: Instructions embedded in external documents or tool responses can change an AI's behavior. Prompts should distinguish instructions from reference material, while code must enforce permissions for data access and tool execution. Tests should distinguish attempted actions, blocked actions, and actual execution, and also check that legitimate tasks are not being blocked.

notes.title: Is multi-agent really better than single-agent?
notes.summary: Splitting work across multiple agents allows them to take on different roles, but also adds calls, information handoffs, and result integration. First identify what a single agent cannot resolve, then compare whether dividing roles solves that problem. The comparison should cover completion rate, response time, cost per successfully completed task, and operational burden.

notes.title: What should an AI agent remember, and when should it forget?
notes.summary: Not holding on to incorrect information matters as much as remembering well. Store information worth using again, and update or stop using information that has become outdated or changed. The design should let users edit and delete memories, and include a way to verify that superseded or deleted information is not reused in later answers.

notes.title: Where should an agent be stopped? — guardrails on input, call counts, and output
notes.summary: Disallowed actions should be blocked before execution, and further execution should be limited once a call budget is reached. Depending on the situation, the agent may need to stop entirely, block a specific action, or wait for approval. It should also determine whether it can answer using information already verified. This note covers input checks, call limits, and output checks with LangChain middleware, along with issues found during implementation.

notes.title: Where should approval go? — a LangChain HITL exercise
notes.summary: Asking users to approve something they have already selected makes them decide twice. Approval should be placed where it is needed, based on an action's impact and reversibility, and users should understand what they are authorizing. This note covers implementing approval, rejection, and resumption with LangChain HITL, along with the errors encountered and how they were resolved.

notes.title: Why build an AI service? — which part of the user's work are you changing
notes.summary: Being able to generate answers with AI isn't a reason to adopt it. I think we need to identify which user task to improve, consider whether it can be solved without AI, and design a flow that lets users recognize and correct errors.

notes.title: How should you choose an LLM? — balancing performance, reasoning, and cost
notes.summary: Before choosing a model, I need to define the answer quality required, acceptable costs and response times, and the consequences of errors. I think models and reasoning settings should be compared on the same tasks, with retries and human review included in the cost of getting a usable result.

notes.title: With DL and LLMs available, why choose traditional ML?
notes.summary: For predictions based on numerical and categorical business data, traditional ML is a useful starting point for comparison. But having little data or tabular inputs is no reason to rule out deep learning or LLMs. I think we need to check how much they improve actual business outcomes and whether that improvement justifies the additional development and operating costs.

notes.title: Why use an sLLM? — not because it's small, but because it fits the requirements
notes.summary: Before choosing an sLLM, I need to check whether it can deliver the quality the task requires. Even a small model can cost more overall if it creates extra review and rework. I think the decision should be based on quality and response time measured with real task inputs, along with costs that include operation and human review.

notes.title: Why is data preprocessing needed, and how far should it go?
notes.summary: The amount of preprocessing needed depends on the condition of the data and its intended use. Filling missing values or splitting documents should preserve the original meaning and the information needed to make decisions. I think it is important to compare results before and after processing to check whether retrieval and answers actually improve.

notes.title: Does Claude Code use my personal settings when called from an app?
notes.summary: Calling a CLI locally can bring personal settings and instructions into the session. I looked into how to exclude settings, disable tools, and stream the response to the screen as it is generated.

notes.title: Why is Python so common in AI development?
notes.summary: Python is widely used because of its rich ecosystem for data processing, model training and experimentation. When connecting an LLM API to an existing service, Java and Spring AI are also options; the choice should account for reuse of existing business logic, team expertise and additional operational overhead.

notes.title: What should an AI agent be given, when, and how much?
notes.summary: Planning an AI agent involves not just its prompt, but what information it needs, when and how much to provide, how long to retain it and what to discard. Deciding what to discard starts with setting criteria for what is worth remembering.

notes.title: 10 prompt techniques — which one to reach for, and when
notes.summary: I think the desired result should guide the choice of prompt technique. I structure the request with RICE, use examples when the output format matters, and Step-back when the premise needs checking.
